model_answer:
A hard breast lump can be caused by benign conditions such as fibroadenoma, breast cyst, infection/abscess, fat necrosis after injury, hormonal breast changes, or breast cancer.  
No, not every breast lump is cancer, but any new lump that is hard, persistent, increasing in size, fixed to the skin/chest, or found in a woman above 40 years must be checked properly.  
She should see a doctor for clinical breast examination and usually breast ultrasound or mammogram, and sometimes a needle test/biopsy to know exactly what it is.  
Women should also watch for nipple discharge especially blood, nipple turning inward, skin dimpling or “orange peel” changes, breast swelling or change in shape, wounds on the breast, persistent redness, or lumps in the armpit.  
Early assessment is important because benign lumps can be treated or monitored, and if it is cancer, early detection gives the best chance of cure.

This is an emergency: fever with worsening yellow eyes/skin, vomiting, shivering and severe headache can be severe malaria with jaundice, hepatitis/liver infection, sepsis, blood breakdown, or other serious infections common in Nigeria.  
Bring your sibling to the hospital immediately for admission/assessment—do not continue home remedies or herbal mixtures, and avoid alcohol or unnecessary drugs because they can worsen the liver.  
We need to check vital signs and do urgent tests: malaria test/blood film, full blood count, blood sugar, liver function and bilirubin, kidney/electrolytes, urine test, hepatitis tests, and possibly blood culture.  
Treatment will depend on the cause, but may include IV fluids, vomiting control, fever control, IV artesunate if severe malaria is suspected/confirmed, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and blood transfusion if there is severe anaemia.  
If they become confused, very weak, stop passing urine, bleed, convulse, or cannot keep any fluid down, treat it as life-threatening and go to the emergency unit now.

A thirty-three-year-old pregnant woman who is seven months pregnant was brought to our hospital by her neighbors. They explained that she suddenly developed severe abdominal pain, and a large amount of blood began to come out from her vagina. Her body was shaking, and she was crying because the pain was intense. Her family said they were afraid that something serious might happen to both the mother and the baby.
Their first question for the doctor was: What could be causing this severe abdominal pain and heavy bleeding?
Their second question was: What should be done immediately for this pregnant woman?
Their third question was: What investigations or tests can be carried out?
Their fourth question was: What treatment is appropriate for her condition?
Their fifth question was: What foods should this pregnant woman avoid, and what hygiene measures should she observe?
model_answer:
This is an obstetric emergency called antepartum haemorrhage; severe painful bleeding at 7 months strongly suggests placental abruption, though placenta praevia or uterine rupture must also be ruled out.  
She should be taken immediately to the labour ward/theatre: call the obstetrician and anaesthetist, check airway/breathing/circulation, give oxygen, insert two large IV lines, start fluids, take blood for urgent transfusion, monitor BP/pulse/urine, and avoid vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded.  
Investigations include packed cell volume/haemoglobin, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile, renal/liver tests, urine protein and BP assessment, ultrasound for placenta and fetal wellbeing, and fetal heart monitoring/CTG if available.  
Treatment depends on mother and baby’s condition: resuscitation and blood transfusion first, then urgent delivery—often by caesarean section if the mother is unstable or the baby is alive/distressed; give anti-D if she is Rh-negative and treat shock or clotting problems.  
She should avoid alcohol, smoking, herbal concoctions, raw/undercooked meat or eggs, unpasteurised milk, and unnecessary drugs, and should maintain good handwashing, perineal hygiene, clean food/water, antenatal visits, and prompt hospital care for any bleeding, pain, fever, or reduced fetal movement.

When the dog bit him, they usually went to their traditional healer; they made an incision on the wound and applied “apọrọ” (traditional preparation) to it. But now, the place where the dog bit him has started producing pus and it is swollen. We explained to them that they should take him to the hospital. Please, what kind of examination can be done for this boy? Can he have rabies because of the dog, even if the dog itself seems to be fine? And what kind of treatment does this young boy need? Consider that the dog did not cause any further injury to his body.
model_answer:
Yes, he must be taken to hospital urgently because pus and swelling mean the wound is infected, and dog bites can also transmit rabies and tetanus.  
The doctor will examine his temperature and general condition, inspect the wound depth and surrounding skin, check for abscess, lymph nodes, nerve/blood vessel injury, and may request wound swab/culture, blood tests, or X-ray if deep injury or foreign body is suspected.  
Rabies is still possible even if the dog looks fine, especially if the dog is unvaccinated or unknown; the dog should be observed for 10 days, but the child should not wait before starting rabies post-exposure treatment.  
Treatment should include thorough washing/cleaning of the wound, drainage if there is an abscess, appropriate antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav, pain relief, and tetanus vaccination/immune globulin depending on his immunization history.  
He also needs rabies vaccine immediately, and rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated around the wound if the bite broke the skin and he has not previously been vaccinated.

question: Adeolu is a 10-year-old child whose mother was my sister. However, for a few days now, I have noticed that this child sits alone ever since his mother died. reference: Adeolu is a ten-year-old child whose mother was my sister. However, for a few days now, I have noticed that this child sits alone ever since his mother died; he does not want to play with anyone, and he does not want to talk to anyone. He has also started refusing to eat, and it looks like he is thinking too much and is heartbroken. This frightened me, so I decided to take him to the hospital for help. And, 'What can I do to help at home, or does this child need to speak to a mental health professional, or what can I do to make him eat or play with his peers, and does he need any medication to help?
model_answer: Yes, Adeolu’s withdrawal, sadness, poor appetite and quietness can be a normal grief reaction after losing his mother, especially in the first days to weeks. At home, give him a calm routine, keep trusted family close, allow him to talk or cry without forcing him, reassure him he is safe and loved, involve him gently in play/school, and offer small frequent favourite meals rather than forcing food. He should see a mental health professional or child psychologist/psychiatrist if he refuses food or drink for long, cannot sleep, talks of wanting to die, becomes very aggressive, hears or sees things, stops functioning at school/home, or the severe withdrawal continues beyond a few weeks. Medication is usually not the first treatment for normal grief; support, counselling, and family care are most important, but a doctor may treat severe depression, anxiety, or sleep problems if diagnosed. Continue follow-up with the hospital, and make sure one stable caregiver stays consistently involved in his daily life.

reference:
A mother living in our neighborhood was pregnant with her second child. At the beginning of the pregnancy, everything was going normally, and she was happy that a new baby was coming. However, a few months ago, she began to experience severe lower abdominal pain. One day, the pain became so intense that she could hardly stand up properly. Shortly afterward, she also started having heavy vaginal bleeding. The bleeding was more than usual, and it made her very weak. When she saw the bleeding, she became frightened that her unborn baby might be in danger. Her husband quickly assisted her to go to the hospital.
My question is: what can cause severe lower abdominal pain during pregnancy? Is heavy bleeding during pregnancy a danger sign for the mother or the unborn baby?
What are the signs that indicate the pregnancy may be in trouble? Is there any medication that can stop the pain and bleeding without harming the unborn baby?
model_answer:
Severe lower abdominal pain in pregnancy can be caused by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental problems such as placenta previa or placental abruption, preterm labour, uterine rupture, fibroids, infections, or even non-pregnancy problems like appendicitis or urinary infection.  
Heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is a serious danger sign for both mother and baby because it can lead to shock, severe anaemia, loss of the pregnancy, premature delivery, or death if not treated urgently.  
Warning signs that pregnancy may be in trouble include heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, dizziness or fainting, fever, severe headache or blurred vision, swelling of face/hands, reduced or no baby movement, leaking fluid, convulsions, or labour pains before term.  
There is no safe “home medicine” that can simply stop pain and bleeding without knowing the cause; she needs urgent hospital assessment with examination, ultrasound, blood tests, fluids/blood if needed, and treatment based on the diagnosis.  
Paracetamol may be used for pain if advised, but she should avoid self-medication, herbal mixtures, aspirin/ibuprofen, or delaying care, because bleeding in pregnancy is an emergency.

question: A guardian of a child observes that the child is coughing intensely, to the extent that the child is being abrupt and struggling to breathe well. What can cause a child to be coughing in abrupt manner? To the extent that the child cannot breathe well and struggling to breathe. What kind of tests can we run for that child? What treatment can we give? And then what advice can we give to the guardian of this child?
reference: A guardian of a child observed that the child is cough intensely, till the end that the child is been abrupt and struggling to breathe well. What can cause a child to be coughing in abrupt manner, till the end that the child can't breathe well, and struggling to breathe? What can kind of test can we run for that child? What treatment can we give? And then what advice can be give to the guardian of this child?
model_answer:
Abrupt intense coughing with difficulty breathing in a child can be caused by choking/foreign body aspiration, asthma attack, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, croup, whooping cough, severe allergy/anaphylaxis, or less commonly TB if cough is prolonged.  
This child needs urgent assessment: check oxygen saturation, temperature, respiratory rate, chest examination, and tests such as chest X-ray, full blood count, blood culture if very ill, sputum/GeneXpert if chronic cough or TB contact, and viral/pertussis tests where available.  
Treatment depends on the cause but may include oxygen, nebulized salbutamol for wheeze/asthma, steroids for asthma/croup, antibiotics for suspected bacterial pneumonia or pertussis, adrenaline for severe allergy, and urgent bronchoscopy/removal if a foreign body is suspected.  
Advise the guardian to take the child to hospital immediately if breathing is difficult, lips are bluish, the child is very weak, cannot feed/talk/cry normally, has chest indrawing, or the cough started suddenly while eating or playing.  
Keep the child sitting upright, avoid smoke/dust, do not give sedating cough syrups or force food/drinks during distress, and ensure immunizations including pertussis and measles vaccines are up to date.

A dog bite can introduce bacteria causing cellulitis/abscess, tetanus, and rabies; rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so prevention must start immediately.  
Wash the wound thoroughly with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes, apply povidone-iodine/chlorhexidine, do not apply herbs or close the wound tightly, and let the hospital clean/debride it properly.  
Because the dog is unvaccinated and roaming, the child needs rabies post-exposure prophylaxis now: rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound if the skin was broken/bleeding.  
The child should also receive tetanus protection according to immunization history, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5–7 days, with pain relief; if penicillin-allergic, the doctor will choose an alternative.  
No blood test can reliably rule out rabies early, but the wound should be assessed for depth, foreign bodies, tendon/nerve injury, and pus, while the dog should be confined and observed by a vet/public health officer for 10 days.

Yes, you should come to the hospital urgently: chills/shivering after childbirth together with foul-smelling vaginal bleeding/discharge suggests puerperal sepsis, often an infection of the womb or retained products of conception.

You need examination, temperature and vital signs, vaginal/wound check, possibly scan, and prompt antibiotics; delay can lead to blood infection and death.  
Do not insert anything into the vagina, change pads frequently, wash hands, and use the cleanest water available for external washing only.

model_answer:
A 3-year-old who does not respond to name or voices and avoids looking at people may have **hearing impairment** or **autism spectrum disorder**, and sometimes **global developmental delay/intellectual disability**.  
Complete immunization and absence of seizures do not rule these out, and vaccines are not a likely cause.  
Possible causes include congenital hearing loss, severe neonatal jaundice, birth asphyxia, prematurity, recurrent ear infections, meningitis, genetic conditions, or autism with no obvious cause.  
The child needs urgent **hearing assessment/audiology**, ear examination by ENT, and developmental assessment by a paediatrician/child neurologist, with referral for speech and behavioural therapy if needed.  
Early diagnosis and intervention greatly improve communication and learning outcomes.

Emergency care is neonatal resuscitation: keep the baby warm and dry, clear the airway only if obstructed, position the head, stimulate gently, give bag-and-mask ventilation if not breathing well, add oxygen as needed, and start chest compressions if the heart rate stays below 60/min despite good ventilation.  
Do not force breastfeeding now; check and treat hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose, start IV fluids, treat seizures if present, and give antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
The baby should be urgently managed in a newborn special care unit/NICU, and if moderate or severe birth asphyxia is confirmed within 6 hours of life, therapeutic cooling may help where available.

question: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother child, and what kind of care can be given to this child?

The child is likely having a **febrile convulsion (fever-related seizure)**, common in children 6 months to 5 years, but in Nigeria fever may be due to **malaria, infection, meningitis, or sepsis**, so the cause must be checked.  
Lay the child **on the side**, keep the child away from sharp objects, loosen tight clothing, and **do not put anything in the mouth** or try to force the child to stop shaking.  
If the convulsion lasts **more than 5 minutes**, repeats, or the child does not wake up well afterward, go to the **nearest hospital immediately** or call emergency help.  
At the hospital, health workers may check blood sugar, malaria test, temperature, and signs of meningitis, and may give medicines like **diazepam/lorazepam** if the seizure continues, plus treatment for the fever cause.  
After the child is awake, give fluids/breastfeed if able and use **paracetamol** for fever, but avoid self-medicating with strong drugs or herbal mixtures.

He should go to a healthcare facility urgently for tests: random/fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, urine test for glucose/ketones/protein, kidney function/electrolytes, blood pressure check, weight/BMI, and possibly cholesterol; other causes like urinary infection, kidney disease, diabetes insipidus, high calcium, and some medicines can also cause similar symptoms.

This is a neonatal emergency: refusal to feed, severe sleepiness/floppiness, absent movement/reflexes and a cold body suggest serious illness such as neonatal sepsis/meningitis, severe hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, birth-related brain injury, or metabolic disease—not just “ordinary breastfeeding refusal.”

Routine immunizations should be postponed for today because the baby is severely ill; stabilize and treat first, then give the missed newborn vaccines before discharge or as soon as clinically stable.

Life-threatening causes that need urgent care include severe asthma attack, pneumonia/sepsis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, heart attack, severe COPD flare, collapsed lung, choking/airway blockage, and coughing blood.  
Danger signs are: difficulty breathing at rest, inability to speak full sentences, bluish lips/fingers, chest pain, confusion or fainting, noisy breathing/wheezing that is worsening, coughing blood, high fever, fast breathing, swollen legs, severe weakness, or oxygen level below 92% if checked.  
He should be taken to a hospital promptly for examination, oxygen check, chest X-ray, sputum test including TB test, blood tests, ECG/heart assessment, and treatment based on the cause; if any danger sign appears, go to emergency immediately.

Bleeding two weeks after delivery can be normal lochia, but increasing bleeding, clots or “flesh/tissue” coming out, bad smell, fever, weakness, or lower abdominal pain may mean retained placenta/products, womb infection, postpartum haemorrhage, or rarely womb/cervix prolapse, so she should go to the hospital urgently.  
Lower abdominal pain after childbirth can be normal mild womb contraction, especially during breastfeeding, but pain with fever, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding, or tenderness is a danger sign of infection.  
Other danger signs after delivery include soaking pads quickly, dizziness/fainting, severe headache or blurred vision, convulsions, chest pain or breathlessness, painful swollen leg, painful breast with fever, and sadness/confusion or thoughts of harming herself or the baby.  
To prevent these problems, she should deliver and do postnatal care with skilled health workers, keep the genital area clean, change pads often, avoid inserting herbs/cloth/fingers into the vagina, take prescribed antibiotics/iron or other medicines correctly, breastfeed, eat well, and rest.  
She should not manage this at home; she needs examination, checking of her womb and blood loss, and possibly scan, medicines, or removal of retained tissue if present.

This sounds like normal labour pain: the womb is contracting and the cervix is opening so the baby can come out, and in first-time mothers labour can be long and very painful.  
The most important thing is that she remains in the hospital where they can monitor her blood pressure, bleeding, the baby’s heartbeat, the progress of cervical opening, and whether her waters have broken.  
A baby being too big for the birth canal is possible, but doctors usually suspect this if labour is not progressing despite strong contractions, the baby’s head is not coming down, or the baby becomes distressed.  
If they find that the baby cannot come safely through the birth canal, or there is fetal distress, severe bleeding, high blood pressure/eclampsia, or prolonged labour, they may advise a Caesarean section to save mother and baby.  
Please encourage her to cooperate with the nurses and doctors, do not take her home, and ask the team clearly about her cervical dilation, baby’s heartbeat, and whether normal delivery is still safe.

This is postpartum haemorrhage, most commonly caused by uterine atony, where the uterus fails to contract, but other causes include retained placenta/products or an undelivered second twin, cervical/vaginal/perineal tears, uterine rupture/inversion, or clotting problems.  
Act immediately: call for help, check vital signs, give oxygen if available, insert two wide-bore IV lines, start rapid IV fluids/blood if available, catheterize the bladder, massage the uterus firmly, and check that the placenta is complete and that no second baby or retained tissue remains.  
Give uterotonics urgently: oxytocin 10 IU IM or slow IV, then oxytocin infusion; also give tranexamic acid 1 g IV as soon as possible, and if bleeding continues use misoprostol 800–1000 mcg rectally/sublingually or ergometrine 0.2 mg IM/IV if she is not hypertensive.  
Examine the birth canal with good light and repair any cervical or vaginal tear; if the uterus is still soft, continue bimanual uterine compression and consider uterine balloon tamponade if trained and equipment is available.  
If bleeding does not stop quickly, the woman is shocked, blood is needed, retained placenta cannot be removed safely, or surgery may be required, arrange urgent referral to a larger hospital while continuing resuscitation, uterotonics, uterine massage/compression, and IV fluids during transfer.

She should eat balanced meals with enough protein, fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and fluids, and attend antenatal clinic regularly because the medicine dose must be monitored to protect both mother and baby.

This is an emergency until proven otherwise: postpartum haemorrhage or shock from hidden/obvious bleeding is a major concern, especially after a very rapid delivery, but also check blood pressure for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia and blood sugar for hypoglycaemia.  

Do not focus on giving food now; assess ABCs, pulse, BP, oxygen saturation, uterine tone, vaginal bleeding, placenta completeness, and look for cervical/vaginal tears or retained products.  

Start two wide-bore IV lines, give IV fluids, massage the uterus, give oxytocin, and if bleeding is suspected give tranexamic acid within 3 hours while arranging urgent Hb/PCV, blood grouping and cross-match.  

Give blood transfusion if she is in shock, has ongoing significant bleeding, or has severe/symptomatic anaemia; do not wait for food to “restore strength.”  

She should be reviewed urgently by the most senior clinician/obstetric team available and monitored closely, because dizziness, dim vision and marked weakness after delivery can rapidly become fatal if due to haemorrhage or severe hypertension.

A newborn who did not cry well and is unusually sleepy soon after birth must be treated as a possible emergency, even if breathing and temperature look normal; causes include birth asphyxia/poor oxygen during delivery, effects of drugs given to the mother such as opioids or magnesium sulphate, low blood sugar, infection, prematurity, or brain injury.  
The baby should be assessed immediately by the neonatal team: check Apgar score, oxygen saturation, blood sugar, heart rate, tone/reflexes, and signs of sepsis, while keeping the baby warm and ensuring the airway and breathing are adequate.  
Treatment depends on the cause and may include stimulation, oxygen or bag-mask ventilation if needed, early breastfeeding or expressed breast milk, IV dextrose for low sugar, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and close observation/admission in the newborn unit.  
At home, the mother should not give the baby water, glucose water, herbs, antibiotics, sedatives, or any medicine unless prescribed; she should return urgently if the baby is not feeding well, becomes floppy, has fever/low temperature, convulsions, fast/difficult breathing, jaundice, or persistent sleepiness.  
The mother should eat a balanced diet with enough fluids—rice/yam/beans/maize, vegetables, fruits, fish/meat/eggs, groundnuts, and continue exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months if the baby is stable and able to feed.

model_answer:
Bluish lips in a newborn, especially during breastfeeding, means low oxygen in the blood (cyanosis) and is a dangerous emergency; it can be caused by serious congenital heart disease, lung infection/pneumonia, aspiration of milk, airway blockage, sepsis, or poor feeding coordination, while liver disease usually causes yellow eyes/skin, not sudden breathlessness during sucking.  
Difficulty breathing or “going lifeless” while feeding is very serious because feeding increases the baby’s oxygen demand, and babies with heart or lung problems may become tired, stop sucking, turn blue, sweat, or breathe fast.  
Other danger signs include fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, flaring nostrils, poor feeding, repeated vomiting, fever or low body temperature, convulsions, extreme sleepiness, limpness, jaundice in the first 24 hours or worsening jaundice, reduced urine, and any blue tongue or lips.  
At home, stop feeding immediately, keep the baby warm, place the baby on the side or upright, gently clear visible milk/mucus from the mouth/nose, and go to the nearest hospital immediately; if the baby is not breathing, start infant CPR if trained.  
In hospital, emergency treatment may include oxygen, suctioning, checking blood sugar and temperature, antibiotics if infection is suspected, chest X-ray/echocardiography, and urgent referral to a neonatal unit or paediatric cardiologist if a heart defect is suspected.

question: A woman was brought to the hospital this morning because she was bleeding heavily and this had caused her a great deal of distress. Heavy bleeding 6 weeks after the last period could be from pregnancy complications such as threatened/incomplete miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy, but also from fibroids, hormonal abnormal uterine bleeding, infection, polyps, bleeding disorders, or rarely cancer.  
Emergency care is ABC assessment, check pulse/BP, lay her flat, give oxygen if needed, insert two wide-bore IV lines, send blood urgently for PCV/FBC, grouping and cross-match, and start IV normal saline/Ringer’s lactate while arranging blood transfusion if she is pale, shocked, or PCV is low.  
Do a urine/serum pregnancy test immediately, speculum and pelvic examination if safe, and urgent pelvic ultrasound to confirm miscarriage, retained products, ectopic pregnancy, fibroid, or other pelvic cause; also check coagulation profile, platelets, renal/liver tests as available.  
While awaiting results, tranexamic acid can be given to reduce bleeding, but definitive treatment depends on the cause: misoprostol or manual vacuum aspiration for incomplete miscarriage, urgent surgery for ruptured ectopic pregnancy, and high-dose hormonal treatment for severe non-pregnancy-related uterine bleeding.  
If bleeding continues or she is unstable, involve a gynaecologist immediately for evacuation of the uterus, uterine tamponade, surgery, and blood transfusion—these are lifesaving measures.

She needs urgent hospital treatment now: check vital signs, blood level and grouping/crossmatch, IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, oxytocin or misoprostol to contract the womb, and strong antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
The doctor must also examine the womb and birth canal, and may need ultrasound, removal of retained tissue/clots, repair of tears, or surgery if bleeding does not stop.  
Do not rely only on injections at home—delay can lead to death from bleeding or sepsis.

Yes, the baby can survive, especially since she cried and was given oxygen quickly, but she must be closely monitored in a newborn/Special Care Baby Unit.
